subject: Mathematics
title: Sequences and Series
learningOutcomes: Recognise a sequence as a function on the natural numbers and distinguish a sequence from a series.
Solve problems on arithmetic sequences and series up to \(n\) terms using \(a_n=a+(n-1)d\) and \(S_n=\frac n2[2a+(n-1)d]\).
Insert arithmetic means between two numbers and find the arithmetic mean of two numbers.
Solve problems on geometric sequences and series up to \(n\) terms using \(a_n=ar^{n-1}\) and \(S_n=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}\).
Identify a sequence as arithmetic or geometric from its terms.
Insert geometric means between two numbers and find the geometric mean \(\sqrt{ab}\).
Find the sum to infinity \(S_\infty=\frac{a}{1-r}\) of a G.P. with \(|r|<1\) and write a recurring decimal as a fraction.
Solve problems on harmonic sequences, harmonic means and the relation \(G^2=AH\).
Recognise sigma \((\Sigma)\) notation and use its properties.
Find \(\Sigma n\), \(\Sigma n^2\) and \(\Sigma n^3\) and use them to sum a series given by its general term.
Sum a series by telescoping, writing each term as a difference of two terms.
Define an arithmetico-geometric series and find its sum to \(n\) terms and to infinity.
Solve real-life problems on arithmetic and geometric sequences, such as savings, seating, compound interest, population and depreciation.

sections.heading: Sequences and Series
sections.body: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers \(a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots\), that is, a function whose domain is the natural numbers. A sequence with a last term is finite; one that goes on forever is infinite. A series is the sum of the terms of a sequence, and \(S_n=a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n\) is the sum of the first \(n\) terms. The two are linked by \(a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\) for \(n\ge2\) and \(a_1=S_1\).

sections.heading: Arithmetic Progression (A.P.)
sections.body: In an A.P. every term is the previous one plus a fixed common difference \(d\). The \(n\)th term is \(a_n=a+(n-1)d\). The sum of \(n\) terms is \(S_n=\dfrac n2[2a+(n-1)d]=\dfrac n2(a+l)\), where \(l\) is the last term. The arithmetic mean of \(a\) and \(b\) is \(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\). To insert \(n\) arithmetic means between \(a\) and \(b\) there are \(n+1\) equal steps, so \(d=\dfrac{b-a}{n+1}\). The sum of the first \(n\) odd numbers is \(n^2\).

sections.heading: Geometric Progression (G.P.)
sections.body: In a G.P. every term is the previous one times a fixed common ratio \(r\). The \(n\)th term is \(a_n=ar^{n-1}\). The sum of \(n\) terms is \(S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}\) for \(r\ne1\), and \(S_n=na\) for \(r=1\). The geometric mean of two positive numbers is \(\sqrt{ab}\). To insert \(n\) geometric means between \(a\) and \(b\), use \(r^{n+1}=\dfrac ba\).

sections.heading: Sum to Infinity and Recurring Decimals
sections.body: An infinite G.P. has a sum only when \(|r|<1\), and then \(S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\). If \(|r|\ge1\) the partial sums do not settle down, so there is no sum. A recurring decimal is an infinite G.P.: \(0.\overline{3}=\dfrac{0.3}{1-0.1}=\dfrac13\) and \(0.4\overline{8}=\dfrac{4}{10}+\dfrac{8}{90}=\dfrac{22}{45}\). Likewise a bouncing ball dropped from height \(h\) that rebounds to \(e\) times its previous height travels \(h\dfrac{1+e}{1-e}\) in all.

sections.heading: Harmonic Progression (H.P.)
sections.body: A sequence is a harmonic progression when the reciprocals of its terms form an A.P. So \(a_n=\dfrac{1}{A+(n-1)D}\), where \(A\) and \(D\) are the first term and common difference of the reciprocal A.P. No term of an H.P. can be zero. The harmonic mean of \(a\) and \(b\) is \(H=\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}\). For two positive numbers the three means satisfy \(G^2=AH\) and \(A\ge G\ge H\), with equality only when the numbers are equal. To insert \(n\) harmonic means, insert \(n\) arithmetic means between the reciprocals and flip back.

sections.heading: Sigma Notation and Power Sums
sections.body: The symbol \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_k\) means \(a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n\). Constants come out of the sum and a sum of terms splits: \(\sum(ca_k+b_k)=c\sum a_k+\sum b_k\), and \(\sum_{k=1}^{n}c=nc\). A sum from \(k=0\) to \(n\) has \(n+1\) terms. The standard results are \(\sum k=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\), \(\sum k^2=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\) and \(\sum k^3=\left[\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2\). To sum a series given by a polynomial in \(k\), split it and use these three results.

sections.heading: Telescoping Sums
sections.body: When each term can be written as a difference, most terms cancel. For example \(\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}=\dfrac1k-\dfrac1{k+1}\), so \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}=1-\dfrac{1}{n+1}=\dfrac{n}{n+1}\). Similarly \(\dfrac{1}{k(k+2)}=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1k-\dfrac1{k+2}\right)\), where the middle terms cancel in steps of two.

sections.heading: Arithmetico-Geometric Series
sections.body: An arithmetico-geometric series has terms of the form (A.P. term) \(\times\) (G.P. term): \(a+(a+d)r+(a+2d)r^2+\cdots\). To sum it, write \(S\), multiply by \(r\) to get \(rS\), and subtract. The terms left over form a G.P. For \(|r|<1\) the sum to infinity is \(S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}+\dfrac{dr}{(1-r)^2}\).

sections.heading: Real-Life Applications
sections.body: Equal yearly additions follow an A.P.: monthly savings that rise by a fixed amount, or seats in rows that increase by a fixed number. Equal percentage changes follow a G.P.: compound interest \(A=P(1+i)^t\), population growth, and depreciation \(V=P(1-i)^t\). Decide first whether each step adds a fixed amount (A.P.) or multiplies by a fixed factor (G.P.), then apply the matching formula.

definitions.definition: An ordered list of numbers \(a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots\), a function on the natural numbers.
A finite sequence has a last term; an infinite sequence has no last term.
The sum of the terms of a sequence; \(S_n\) is the sum of the first \(n\) terms.
A sequence in which the difference between consecutive terms is a constant \(d\).
The number \(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\) that makes \(a\), the mean and \(b\) an A.P.
A sequence in which the ratio of consecutive terms is a constant \(r\).
The number \(\sqrt{ab}\) that makes \(a\), the mean and \(b\) a G.P. (for positive \(a,b\)).
The value \(\dfrac{a}{1-r}\) that the partial sums of a G.P. approach when \(|r|<1\).
A sequence whose reciprocals form an A.P.
The number \(\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}\); the reciprocal of the A.M. of \(\frac1a\) and \(\frac1b\).
A sum whose terms are differences, so that the middle terms cancel.
A series whose terms are the product of an A.P. term and a G.P. term.
A decimal with a block of digits that repeats forever, for example \(0.\overline{27}\); it equals a fraction.

examTips: In \(a_n=a+(n-1)d\) the multiplier of \(d\) is \(n-1\), not \(n\). For a G.P. the power of \(r\) is \(n-1\).
When two terms are given, subtract them to find \(d\) first: \(a_q-a_p=(q-p)d\). For a G.P. divide: \(\dfrac{a_q}{a_p}=r^{q-p}\).
Use \(S_n=\dfrac n2(a+l)\) when the last term is known, and \(S_n=\dfrac n2[2a+(n-1)d]\) when it is not.
Inserting \(n\) means between \(a\) and \(b\) gives \(n+2\) terms in all, so \(b\) is the \((n+2)\)th term and the number of steps is \(n+1\).
Check \(|r|<1\) before using \(S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\). If \(|r|\ge1\), say there is no sum.
For a recurring decimal such as \(0.4\overline{8}\), separate the part that does not repeat: \(\dfrac{4}{10}+\dfrac{8}{90}\).
To work with an H.P., flip every term to get an A.P., solve, and flip the answer back. Never add H.P. terms with the A.P. formulas directly.
A sum from \(k=0\) to \(n\) has \(n+1\) terms, and \(\sum_{k=1}^{n}c=nc\), not \(c\).
Quick check on means: \(G^2=AH\), and for unequal positive numbers \(A>G>H\).
For an arithmetico-geometric series multiply by \(r\) and subtract; do not forget the G.P. that remains in the middle and the last term for a finite sum.
